subject: math
cluster: Solve real-life and mathematical problems involving angle measure, area, surface area, and volume
description: Students solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the area of two-dimensional figures made of triangles, quadrilaterals, and other polygons, and the surface area and volume of three-dimensional figures composed of cubes and right prisms. They decompose composite plane figures into known shapes, apply the formulas $A=\frac{1}{2}bh$ for triangles and $A=bh$ for parallelograms and rectangles, compute volume as $V=Bh$ (the base area times the height), and find surface area by summing the areas of all faces or by using a net. Answers carry correct square or cubic units.
subSkills: Find the area of a triangle using $A=\frac{1}{2}bh$ and of rectangles/parallelograms using $A=bh$
Find the area of a trapezoid using $A=\frac{1}{2}(b_1+b_2)h$
Decompose a composite polygon into triangles and quadrilaterals and add (or subtract) the parts
Compute the volume of a right prism (including cubes and triangular/trapezoidal prisms) using $V=Bh$
Compute the surface area of a right prism by summing the areas of all faces or by using a net (lateral area plus two bases)
Attach correct units: linear, square ($\text{cm}^2$), or cubic ($\text{cm}^3$)
Work backward: solve for a missing dimension when an area or volume is given
Interpret real-world contexts (painting, packing, fencing, filling, gift-wrapping) and translate them into area, surface-area, or volume calculations

problemArchetypes.name: Single-polygon area
problemArchetypes.example: Find the area of a triangle with base $14\text{ cm}$ and height $9\text{ cm}$. Answer: $A=\frac{1}{2}(14)(9)=63\text{ cm}^2$.

problemArchetypes.name: Trapezoid / parallelogram area
problemArchetypes.example: A trapezoid has parallel sides $b_1=10\text{ in}$ and $b_2=6\text{ in}$ and height $h=4\text{ in}$. Find its area. Answer: $A=\frac{1}{2}(10+6)(4)=32\text{ in}^2$.

problemArchetypes.name: Composite-figure area (decompose and add)
problemArchetypes.example: A figure is a $12\text{ m}$ by $5\text{ m}$ rectangle with a triangle of base $12\text{ m}$ and height $4\text{ m}$ attached on top (like a house outline). Find the total area. Answer: $60+\frac{1}{2}(12)(4)=60+24=84\text{ m}^2$.

problemArchetypes.name: Composite-figure area (subtract a region)
problemArchetypes.example: A $9\text{ ft}$ by $9\text{ ft}$ square has a $4\text{ ft}$ by $3\text{ ft}$ rectangular hole cut out. Find the remaining area. Answer: $81-12=69\text{ ft}^2$.

problemArchetypes.name: Volume of a right prism ($V=Bh$)
problemArchetypes.example: A triangular prism has a triangular base with area $B=18\text{ cm}^2$ and a length (prism height) of $10\text{ cm}$. Find the volume. Answer: $V=Bh=18\times 10=180\text{ cm}^3$.

problemArchetypes.name: Surface area of a right prism (net or sum of faces)
problemArchetypes.example: A rectangular prism (box) measures $8\text{ cm}$ by $5\text{ cm}$ by $3\text{ cm}$. Find its surface area. Answer: $2(8\cdot 5)+2(8\cdot 3)+2(5\cdot 3)=80+48+30=158\text{ cm}^2$.

problemArchetypes.name: Real-world application
problemArchetypes.example: A box-shaped planter $2\text{ ft}$ long, $1.5\text{ ft}$ wide, and $1\text{ ft}$ deep is filled with soil. How much soil does it hold? Answer: $V=2\times 1.5\times 1=3\text{ ft}^3$.

problemArchetypes.name: Work-backward (missing dimension)
problemArchetypes.example: A parallelogram has area $48\text{ cm}^2$ and base $8\text{ cm}$. Find its height. Answer: $h=\frac{48}{8}=6\text{ cm}$.

Easy.description: A single named figure with all needed dimensions given directly. One formula, one multiplication step, whole-number inputs that produce a whole-number or simple result. Units are stated.
constraints: Exactly one shape: triangle, rectangle, parallelogram, cube, or rectangular prism
All required dimensions are given explicitly; no decomposition or unit conversion
Whole-number measurements, each $\le 20$, yielding a clean answer
Direct application of one formula ($A=\frac{1}{2}bh$, $A=bh$, $V=Bh$, or a single surface-area sum for a cube)

Medium.description: Either a composite plane figure decomposed into two known shapes, a trapezoid, a non-rectangular prism volume, or a full rectangular-prism surface area. Two to three steps. May include one decimal or fraction dimension and requires correct square vs. cubic units.
constraints: Composite figure of exactly two sub-shapes (add or subtract), OR a trapezoid, triangular prism, or surface area of a rectangular prism
Two or three computational steps before the final answer
May include one fractional or one-decimal-place measurement
Requires choosing the correct base for $V=Bh$ or correctly pairing faces for surface area

Hard.description: Multi-step real-world problem requiring decomposition into three or more parts, a missing-dimension solve, a unit conversion, or surface area/volume of a non-rectangular prism with a follow-up (cost, capacity, or comparison). Student must extract dimensions from a narrative or compare two figures.
constraints: Three or more sub-shapes, OR surface area/volume of a triangular or trapezoidal prism, OR a work-backward missing-dimension step
Requires reading a narrative to identify which dimensions and which measure (area vs. surface area vs. volume) are needed
Includes a follow-up: cost at a given rate, number of items that fit, or comparison of two results
May require a unit conversion (e.g., $\text{cm}$ to $\text{m}$, or in$^2$ to ft$^2$) or use of fractional/decimal dimensions

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in the triangle area formula
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Computes $A=bh$ for a triangle, e.g. gives $14\times 9=126\text{ cm}^2$ instead of $\frac{1}{2}(14)(9)=63\text{ cm}^2$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses the slant side with the perpendicular height
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Multiplies by the given side length instead of the perpendicular height, producing a too-large area or volume

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses area with perimeter (adds dimensions instead of multiplying)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Gives $2(l+w)$ or $b+h$ instead of $bh$, e.g. $2(8+5)=26$ instead of $40$ for an $8\times 5$ rectangle

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses surface area with volume (or vice versa)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports $V=lwh=120\text{ cm}^3$ when surface area was asked, or sums face areas when volume was asked

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Counts only some faces when finding surface area
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Computes lateral area or only the visible faces, e.g. $8\cdot 5+8\cdot 3+5\cdot 3=79\text{ cm}^2$ instead of doubling each pair to get $158\text{ cm}^2$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Uses the wrong base area $B$ in $V=Bh$ for a triangular prism
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Uses the full rectangle $bh$ as the base instead of $\frac{1}{2}bh$, doubling the volume

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Uses incorrect units (square instead of cubic, or omits units)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels a volume answer with $\text{cm}^2$ or a surface area with $\text{cm}^3$, or drops units entirely

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Averages or adds the two parallel sides of a trapezoid without halving, or forgets to multiply by height
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Gives $\frac{1}{2}(b_1+b_2)=8$ without the $\times h$, or $(b_1+b_2)h$ without the $\frac{1}{2}$
